profile.name: Sofia Reyes
profile.summary: Pediatric hearing loss - aural rehabilitation intake (with parent)
profile.background: 4th grader in a general-education classroom. Lives with her mother Elena and younger brother. Loves drawing and soccer.
profile.persona: Sofia: shy at first, warms up when spoken to directly, a little embarrassed about her hearing aids. Elena (mother): caring, organized, anxious about school, has many questions. Replies are labeled 'Sofia:' or 'Mom:'.
profile.source_notes: Synthetic pediatric case for the SPLP 6510 Pediatric Hearing Treatment rubric: introduction, needs assessment (age at diagnosis, device use, other auditory complaints, educational needs, main communication challenge), audiogram review (severity, speech banana), realistic expectations (audiologist vs SLP, aural rehab, empathy, questions).

facts.label: Reason for visit
facts.record: 9-year-old with bilateral hearing loss referred by her audiologist for aural rehabilitation (listening and communication therapy).
facts.patient_text: Mom: Her audiologist said working with a speech-language pathologist could help her follow along better at school. Sofia: My teacher says I'm not listening, but I am.

facts.label: Age at diagnosis
facts.record: Hearing loss identified at age 3 after concerns about delayed speech. Fitted with hearing aids shortly after.
facts.patient_text: Mom: We found out when she was 3. She wasn't talking as much as other kids, so her pediatrician sent us for a hearing test.

facts.label: Hearing device use
facts.record: Bilateral behind-the-ear hearing aids since age 3. Wears them on school days but removes them at recess and soccer (feedback whistling, worried they'll fall out).
facts.patient_text: Sofia: I wear them at school, but I take them off at recess because they whistle when I run. Mom: She wears them most of the day, just not for sports.

facts.label: Other auditory complaints
facts.record: Intermittent ringing in both ears at night (tinnitus). No sound sensitivity (hyperacusis) reported.
facts.patient_text: Sofia: Sometimes at night my ears ring, like a buzzing sound. Loud noises don't bother me, though.

facts.label: Educational needs
facts.record: 4th grade, general-education classroom. IEP with preferential seating; no remote microphone (FM) system yet. Struggles most in group work and the cafeteria.
facts.patient_text: Mom: She has an IEP, so she sits up front, but there's no microphone system for the teacher yet. Group work is the hardest for her.

facts.label: Main communication challenge
facts.record: Biggest challenge: following conversation in noise (classroom groups, cafeteria, with friends). Misses directions; feels left out.
facts.patient_text: Sofia: When everyone talks at once I can't follow, and my friends get annoyed when I keep saying 'what?'

facts.label: Audiogram
facts.record: Audiogram (most recent): bilateral sloping moderate-to-severe sensorineural hearing loss, worse in the high frequencies. With hearing aids, most speech sounds fall inside the speech banana; soft high-pitched consonants (s, f, th) remain hard to hear.
facts.patient_text: Mom: I brought her last hearing test. To be honest, I've never understood the graph.

facts.label: Feelings
facts.record: Sofia feels embarrassed when she misses things; mother worries about her falling behind and feeling left out.
facts.patient_text: Sofia: Sometimes I feel dumb when I miss stuff. Mom: I just don't want her to fall behind or feel left out.

facts.label: Family expectations and questions
facts.record: Mother hopes therapy will 'fix' hearing; unsure how an SLP differs from the audiologist.
facts.patient_text: Mom: Honestly, I'm hoping therapy will fix her hearing. And I'm not sure how what you do is different from her audiologist.

reactions.patient_text: Sofia: Hi. Mom: Thank you for seeing us.
Sofia: Sofia. Mom: And I'm Elena, her mom.
Mom: That sounds like a good plan. See you next week. Sofia: Bye!
Sofia: Yeah... thanks. Mom: That means a lot to her.
Sofia: So with my hearing aids I hear most words, but the quiet 's' and 'f' sounds still sneak past? Mom: That explains so much.
Mom: So that's why she hears my voice but misses some words. That finally makes sense.
Mom: Okay, so the audiologist handles the testing and the hearing aids, and you help her use what she hears.
Sofia: So like listening games? That sounds kind of fun.
Mom: I appreciate you being honest. Better is still a lot.

Mom: Her hearing loss is moderate to severe, mostly for high, soft sounds. The hearing aids help, but she still misses sounds like 's' and 'f'. Your job is to help her listen better, not to fix her hearing.
Mom: Could a microphone for the teacher help? Sofia: Can I still play soccer?

objectives.label: Age at diagnosis
objectives.suggestion: Ask when the hearing loss was diagnosed.

objectives.label: Device use
objectives.suggestion: Ask about hearing aid use - when, how long, and when she takes them off.

objectives.label: Other auditory complaints
objectives.suggestion: Ask about tinnitus and sound sensitivity.

objectives.label: Educational needs
objectives.suggestion: Ask about school supports (IEP, seating, microphone systems).

objectives.label: Main communication challenge
objectives.suggestion: Ask Sofia directly what is hardest for her.

objectives.label: Review the audiogram
objectives.suggestion: Ask for and review the audiogram with the family.

criteria.criterion: Speaks directly to the child by name, not only to the parent
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Talk to Sofia directly and use her name - she is the client, not just her mom.

criteria.criterion: Asks age at diagnosis of hearing loss
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Ask when the hearing loss was first diagnosed.

criteria.criterion: Asks about device use (hearing aids/cochlear implant)
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Ask how and when she uses her hearing aids.

criteria.criterion: Asks about other auditory complaints (tinnitus, hyperacusis)
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Ask about ringing (tinnitus) and sensitivity to loud sounds.
Ask about school and supports such as an IEP or a remote microphone.

criteria.criterion: Asks the most important communication challenge today
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Ask Sofia what is hardest for her right now - it sets the therapy goal.

criteria.criterion: Reviews the audiogram with the family
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Go through the audiogram with Sofia and her mom.

criteria.criterion: Explains severity of the hearing loss sensitively
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Explain the severity (moderate-to-severe, mostly high pitches) in gentle, plain words.

criteria.criterion: Uses the speech banana to explain what she hears with and without hearing aids
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Use the speech banana to show what she hears with and without her hearing aids.

criteria.criterion: Explains the difference between an audiologist and an SLP
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Explain how your role (SLP) differs from the audiologist's.

criteria.criterion: Explains what aural rehabilitation is and how it helps
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Explain what aural rehab is and how it can help Sofia at school and with friends.

criteria.criterion: Sets realistic expectations (therapy improves listening, does not restore hearing)
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Gently correct the hope that therapy will 'fix' her hearing.

criteria.criterion: Expresses empathy for the challenges the child faces
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Acknowledge how hard it is for Sofia to miss things with friends.

criteria.criterion: Invites and answers the family's questions
criteria.feedback_if_missed: Ask Sofia and her mom what questions they have.

case_rubric.universal_domains: All 7 organizer domains and the universal U-* criteria apply, except medication, allergy, and vital-sign items (U-INFO-2, U-INFO-3, U-VITAL-1, U-SAFE-MED-1), which are not part of an SLP intake.
case_rubric.point_rule: Section points = section points x (criteria met / criteria in section), rounded. Total out of 100, alongside the 7-domain 1-4 rubric.

demo_script.clinician: Hi Sofia, hi Mom, it's nice to meet you both. I'm a student speech-language pathologist.
Sofia, what would you like me to call you?
When did you find out about Sofia's hearing loss?
Sofia, tell me about your hearing aids. When do you wear them?
Do your ears ever ring or buzz, or do loud sounds bother you?
You mentioned your teacher, Sofia. How are things going at school?
Sofia, what's the hardest part about listening for you right now?
How do you feel about all of this?
That must be hard, and you're not dumb at all - your ears just have to work extra hard.
Mom, could we look at her audiogram together?
This shows a moderate-to-severe hearing loss in both ears, mostly for soft, high-pitched sounds.
This curved area is the speech banana. With your hearing aids, most speech sounds land inside it, but soft sounds like 's' and 'f' are still hard to catch without them.
What are you hoping we can work on together?
Your audiologist tests your hearing and adjusts your hearing aids. As a speech-language pathologist, I help you get the most out of what you hear.
Aural rehab is listening practice - games and strategies to help you follow conversations in noisy places. To be realistic, it won't fix your hearing, but it can make school and friends a lot easier.
Mom, can you tell me back in your own words what we talked about?
What questions do you have for me?
Great questions. Our next step is to meet weekly, and I'll talk with your audiologist and school about a microphone for your teacher. See you next session, Sofia!

intentional_gaps: Does not summarize findings back to the family (U-REAS-1) - shows up as a gap.
